title: Quoting Terk Terkowitz
content:
If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions. An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.

— Terk Terkowitz, An update from Amazon engineering leadership on the role of the developer in the age of AI

title: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
content:
Many people think1 that getting “good at AI” is trivial. Sure, with some early models there were tricks you had to learn,2 but current models don’t need them. Even if there are different tricks3 that work on current models, the next generation will render them obsolete, so why bother? Just tell the model what you want it to do.

This take is particularly popular with the anti-AI crowd, who scoff4 at the idea that AI-reluctant people are being left behind, or that it might be irresponsible to advise other engineers to avoid AI use entirely. According to them, if AI does ever become capable enough to be worth using, they’ll be able to start using it with no learning curve. Is that right?

No. Like most things, getting good at using AI isn’t just about clever tricks. It requires developing long-term skills5, which takes time and practice.

Supplying the right context

One failure mode I’ve seen with people who are new to AI is expecting it to read their mind: for instance, asking it to “solve my issue” without ever saying what the issue is, or asking it about some Slack-related problem without actually connecting your agent to Slack. Agents are flexible and will try their absolute hardest to guess what problem you’re facing and how to solve it, but the guesses will be largely wrong. Skilled AI users will pick up on the fact that the agent is missing key context and backtrack.

Skilled AI users will also reflexively include why they want to achieve their current goal, so that the agent has enough context to make decisions. This is often non-trivial: most of us know what we want to do but have to take a second to think about the broader reasons behind it.

Knowing what the model can and can’t do

AI capabilities are weird: they are very good at some tasks and very bad at others, and it’s hard to predict which task falls into which category. For instance, I know that I can ask an agent to come up with new architectural ideas for how to structure a service, but that I shouldn’t ask it to come up with new features that the service can offer. Worse still, there is a third category6 of tasks that AI models are bad at but can be prompted into being good: for instance, writing PR descriptions.

Of course, this changes with new models, but less than you’d think. In general, new models get much better at the tasks the old models were already good at, and a little better at the tasks the old models sucked at. So developing a sense of what AI can and can’t do is a surprisingly durable skill.

Really internalizing what the model can do is trickier than it sounds. For instance, I initially struggled to set up MCP servers for GitHub Copilot before realizing7 I could just ask Copilot to install its own MCP servers. I now reflexively ask AI agents to do local testing of changes — standing up servers, hammering them with curls, running through variations and edge cases — but it took me a while to realize I could ask for that. I have only just started scheduling a job for 6am my time for an agent to go through messages that have come in from different timezones and do some preliminary investigation. What other capabilities8 am I leaving on the table?

Knowing what mistakes the models make

Reviewing AI-generated code is a substantially different skillset from reviewing human-written code. There are whole categories of bugs — off-by-one errors, for instance — that human-written code is prone to but AI-generated code is not. Similarly, there are mistakes that are rare in human-written code but are very common in AI-generated code. I’ve written about how these tend to be mistakes of misalignment: over-engineering some areas that humans would know aren’t important, or trading off important requirements in order to satisfy made-up ones, and so on.

Reviewers used to human-written code are often dazzled by the superficial fluency of AI-generated code. It’s always exhaustively commented and tested and uses sophisticated language features. If a human programmer produced code like this, you’d be inclined to trust their judgment that a mutex is required in this case — but with an AI programmer, you ought to be very suspicious about new mutexes, which are often introduced to satisfy completely insignificant edge cases.

Rapidly skim-reading AI slop

This skill is kind of silly, but it’s so practically important I have to include it. AI models produce a lot of useful output, but it’s often lost in a thick forest of verbiage. Once you’ve read enough of it, you can sort of just let your eyes flow over the phrasing until you get to the specific claims and evidence. If you’re not used to this, you will waste a lot of time and emotional energy trying to cut through the foliage.

Will these skills be made obsolete too?

It’s possible that these skills are also temporary. Maybe in the future the agent will just do what we want perfectly, freeing us from the need to actually read its output. Maybe model tooling will get good enough to automatically supply the right context, and the models will get good enough to be able to do everything and make no mistakes. Maybe! But that would require the models to get so good that humans aren’t needed at all.

Don’t be a doomer. Like chess, software’s centaur age — the period where a human-machine pairing can beat individual humans or machines — may last decades. Developing skills for the centaur age is still worthwhile, just like it was worthwhile to learn Angular or React even though it seemed likely that those frameworks would be obsolete9 in a decade.

Conclusion

I’ve left a lot of skills out: knowing when to abandon or steer an agent session, how to break work up between agents, when to trust AI claims and when to verify, how to minimize costs by using smaller models, and so on. On top of all that, even though it’s not durably useful to stay up to date with the current set of tricks (plus knowing which model is the best for which tasks), it’s still very useful in the short-term. Keeping up without getting lost is a skill in its own right.

It shouldn’t be surprising that working with AI involves actual skills. It’s like working with a really weird person: a savant with mad skills in some areas and huge gaps in others, a prolific but inexpert communicator, a workaholic with no long-term memory, and so on. If you were a manager and had someone like that as your employee, you could likely get a lot of value out of them, but it would take time10 to figure out how.

If you’re deliberately avoiding using AI, you are likely being left behind by the people who aren’t. If you’re advising other people to avoid AI completely, you are doing them no favors. I do think it’s a mistake to go fully into AI, because LLMs reward expertise, which is best gained by hand. However, if you never practice using AI, you are never going to get good at it.

  1. I see it all the time, most recently here and here (in fairness: that post does think there’s skill involved, just not durable skill).

  2. Like asking it to think step-by-step or saying “you are a skilled software engineer” at the start of the prompt.

    ↩

  3. Like offering moral support.

    ↩

  4. In fact, they often believe that AI users are literally damaging their brains. As I’ve said a few times, I think this idea is mistaken.

    ↩

  5. Incidentally, the reuse of the word “skills” to refer to “job-specific dynamically-loaded prompts” has made this post a nightmare to write.

    ↩

  6. There’s not even consensus on which tasks are in which category. Many people think LLMs are great at writing prompts for other LLMs, but I think they’re terrible (overly prescriptive, etc). This is obscured by the fact that LLMs can manage swarms much more efficiently than humans, but I think most people agree that having a single subagent is worse than just doing it on the main thread.

    ↩

  10. In no small part because you can’t trust their own claims about their abilities.

title: Some thoughts on hosting email
content:
Generally speaking, email isn't as hard as its reputation would suggest. Yes, big-tech providers will occasionally send my messages to spam... but paying for commercial email doesn't guarantee delivery: emails within a single provider are generally safe, but in my experience, big-tech to other big-tech has a ~75% chance.

Because of this, having my own mail server is great for piece of mind: I can be sure that anyone can send me an email without it mysteriously vanishing. My reply might go to spam, but at that point we're already in communication and can sort it out.

A softer version of self hosting is to keep a big-tech account, but only use it for initiating conversations. Point the "reply-to" header at a server you run, and give that address when people ask for contact details.

Since replies to real emails never go to spam, this provides the best of both worlds: maximizing the chance that someone else will get your message, while also maximizing the chance that you will get theirs.

Receiving email requires:

  • A publicly routable IPv4 address
  • Any server: good uptime is not required.
  • A domain [optional]

Despite it being 2026, many mail servers still don't support IPv6: if you have a good ISP, it should be possible to get a public IPv4 address arranged. Otherwise, the only real option is to rent space in a datacenter, which will cost some money.

(Note, there's no requirement for the VPS to actually run the mail daemon: It's possible to have it forwarding traffic to a box in your house)

The server itself doesn't have to be anything special. A "big" email is only a few megabytes, and people only send a few messages per day. However, disk space may be a consideration if you plan on having multiple users.

Mailer daemons will retry message delivery, and only give up after days of downtime. If it does, the sender will get a failure notification: emails will never be dropped silently.

Regarding domains, "ihavenoname@[65.109.172.162]" is a perfectly valid email address. However, doing this ties your identity to your hosting provider or ISP, which is not ideal.

Buying, or rather renting, a domain costs money. It's not a huge amount of money (around 1 $/month), but it is a significant commitment. If you let a domain lapse, someone else can buy it and take over your old address. I prefer to think of the cost as $800 per lifetime: not a prohibitive amount, but you should think twice before getting yet-another domain for a sideproject.

(Just remember that email needs an MX record)

Sending email requires:

  • An IP address with a PTR record
  • A domain

The domain is unavoidable here, because you'll need to make a few DNS records to prove the moral character of your packets. Specifically, you'll need SPF and DKIM. 

; SPF record
@ TXT "v=spf1 ip4:65.109.172.162 ip6:2a01:4f9:c011:841a::1 -all"

SPF tells receiving servers to accept mail from particular IP addresses and reject everything else. Importantly, this means if you have multiple different addresses, the mailer daemon will have to be configured to use a specific one.

Most servers will handle a missing SPF record as "deny everything", which is sensible: otherwise, even if someone had SPF at root, bad actors could spoof emails from a non-existent subdomains.

The second authentication mechanism is DKIM, which uses a cryptographic signing key published through DNS. Here's mine, but you will need to generate your own: 

2020._domainkey TXT "v=DKIM1;h=sha256;k=rsa;p=MIGfMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4GNADCBi
QKBgQDcysWHfXhdjsK3jWRnUKa3cdNF7gfl0EP/Xe2r5Ixqp7htPRVx7sntLgF1S5fODBM9o9xWSTwu
TuuFF0DLvkvi2fiddiSFa+0IXMb7sevhYIGha6Ewpk5h4vHkRIEGG7MDTlnXovgQpq5Q6MUymU6Z+Or
H6xXBaiwf8wOfZtRIYwIDAQAB"

Most providers also require reverse DNS on the origin IP address. This doesn't have to be the same domain as you are sending email from, but it should be a public hostname associated with your server.

Dealing with spam:

Spam hasn't been as much of a problem as I expected, despite my near-worst case setup: a catchall email and a contact address listed on a public website. All I've needed to deal with spam is:

  • SPF checking, but not enforcement. (default allow)
  • Light email obfuscation.
  • A blacklist of 12 domains and IP addresses

I'm not particularly worried about the spoofing potential of allowing unauthenticated messages since I have infinite addresses; If I get an email to my blog's comment box purporting to be a bill from my hosting provider, then I know it's fake regardless of what's in the "From" field or message body.

However, this relaxed SPF does still filter out a lot of the spam: most of the particularly obnoxious spammers forge emails from well known-domains which do have an SPF record.

There are lots of wacky solutions for email obfuscation: images, javascript initiated network requests, encryption, etc, etc. In practice, 99% of spam bots don't parse HTML and can be thrown off by something as simple as: 

<!-- A random comment -->
blog@maurycyz<!--.example-->.com

<!-- Or needless percent encoding -->
<a href=mailto:blog@%6daurycyz.com>email</a>

This works in every browser, is compatible with screen readers and not too hard to figure out by hand. More extreme measures would also work, but why bother?

With blacklists, there is a very long tail needed to get rid of all spam, but it doesn't take much at all to get it down to tolerable levels. For me, it was enough to block seven domains and five IP addresses (not address blocks) to get it down to around 3 messages per week: I think that's a sensible price for being sure nothing important will get caught up.

Security:

Getting your email compromised is bad. Not only does it have a lot of personal information, most services run password resets and account recovery over email.

Some attacks are technical, but many aren't: your server password should not be "password123". If you don't trust yourself to use a good password, set up key-based for authentication.

In terms of defending against exploits, the best thing to do is keep everything up to date and isolated:

Setup automatic updates and check back a moth later to make sure they work. Services should be run as separate unprivileged users: if your web server gets popped, the attacker should not be able to read your email.

One thing that is unique to email is just how aggressive people are be when blacklisting IPs: if your server gets used to send spam, good luck recovering any reputation. Because of this, it's a very good idea to lock down outgoing network traffic.

  • A web server doesn't need to make any outgoing connections.
  • A minecraft server needs HTTPS and DNS to authenticate users, but should not have access to anything else.
  • Only the mail daemon needs outgoing port 25 access.

(Also, make sure to lock down locally submitting email)

Reputation aside, this is good security practice. Remember log4shell, that trivially exploitable RCE against Java applications? It requires downloading a payload from the attacker's server, so proper firewalling makes it impossible to exploit. Additionally, almost all malware opens up a communication channel over the internet: a crypto miner needs to download the blockchain state, a stealer needs to upload the stolen data...

content:

  • Hey look at this: Delights to delectate.

Agents vs ecommerce (permalink)

The first widely read piece of tech criticism I ever wrote was "Metacrap: Putting the torch to the seven strawmen of the meta-utopia," a response to the underlying philosophy of the "Semantic Web" that I published in 2001:

https://people.well.com/user/doctorow/metacrap.htm

The piece holds up surprisingly well today (if I do say so myself), and not just for its criticism of the ontological incoherence of "web semantics." The most relevant concept I develop in that piece is a criticism of any plan that starts with "first, everyone else in the world just needs to set aside their needs and advantages in favor of my priorities, and then my plan will work."

This is especially relevant today in the context of "agentic AI." When this idea was first mooted, the big idea was that you could instruct a chatbot to venture out onto the public, unstructured web and it would do your bidding, for example, finding all the flights that fit your criteria and comparing prices for all of them, picking the best one and booking it for you.

This idea quickly foundered. Each step in that process was too complex and specialized for a single chatbot; so the notion quickly gave way to "swarms" of specialized chatbots – one to search the web and identify likely travel websites; one to search those websites; one to evaluate flights against your criteria, one to handle the transaction, and so on.

Through specialization, these bots could be made far more accurate, but at a price: both the literal price of all the extra computation that goes into powering a "swarm" versus a single process, and the reliability price that arises from complexity. That's because error rates are multiplicative: combine two bots with low failure rates into a single system and that system will have a higher failure rate than any of its components. This compounding error rate only increases as you add more and more bots, so every time you add a new specialized bot to decrease the error rate in its area of specialization, you increase the overall error rate of the system by adding more complexity to it.

Despite this, companies pressed on ahead with "agentic," without any regard to the realities or consequences. For example, Microsoft has repeatedly announced that it will modify Windows to eliminate all forms of PC-side privacy and confidentiality, sending a continuous stream of screenshots to Microsoft's cloud servers so that your Microsoft "agent" can access your private data on Microsoft's cloud:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/06/1000x-liability/#graceful-failure-modes

But the real fix for "agentic" is for everyone in the world to rearrange their affairs to the benefit of AI agents. This is the same demand that the Semantic Web people made in the early oughts, and it has the same problems. The Semantic Web people operated on the assumption that there were freestanding, objectively correct ways of describing things and that everyone who put information on the web would eventually come to see that adopting these correct semantics was to everyone's advantage.

In reality, these semantic differences are the expression of real, serious, unresolvable philosophical, technical, moral and political arguments. The reason that some media outlets won't describe transwomen as women isn't because they lack an appreciation of objectively correct semantic classifications – it's because they're bigots. That's the same reason "race realists" insist that there is a biological category called "race," that exists despite everything computational genomics has proved:

https://pluralistic.net/2020/08/16/combat-wheelchairs/#race-realism

In my book The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI, I predicted that a similar dynamic would play out when it came to agentic AI and websites. The reason websites are so inhospitable to bots is that ecommerce sites don't want to be legible to automated tools:

https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374621568/thereversecentaursguidetolifeafterai/

Ecommerce websites deploy a wide range of sleazy tactics to raise prices, including surveillance pricing:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/07/gouged/#aeropain

They use market power to rig whole categories, forcing prices up:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/15/enshittipedia/

Multiple law-enforcers, Republic and Democrat, state and federal, have sued companies for "drip pricing" and "junk fees" that make it impossible to know what the actual price is until you've spent a long-ass time going through the purchase process:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/07/drip-drip-drip/#drip-off

Surveillance pricing, drip pricing, junk fees, price fixing and "most favored nation" deals are the source of all the growth in profitability by the economy's largest, most important firms. These tactics require opacity and are antithetical to the kinds of automated comparison-shopping that agentic peddlers promise:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities

These tactics are facially illegal and despite this, they are widely practiced. Cheating is so profitable that it's cheaper for firms to buy off regulators and pay fines than it is for them to stop criming. The fantasy that these same companies would welcome agentic shopping bots with open arms is just as implausible as the idea that if we feed enough words to the word-guessing program, it will wake up and become a "super intelligence":

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/18/surprise/#wow-signal

What's more, the AI companies know this. Google's big plan to make AI profitable is to sell merchants the power to combine its surveillance data with its AI tools to price-gouge shoppers:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/21/cod-marxism/#wannamaker-slain

And right on time, ecommerce websites are mass-blocking AI agents:

https://gizmodo.com/online-shopping-platforms-turn-against-third-party-ai-agents-2000831298

They're doing it in part because AI agents allow shoppers to cheat (for example, by renewing a "temporary" hold on a used item to block other buyers indefinitely), but also because they don't want automation tools on their platforms at all. These tools are a frontal assault on all the most exciting (and sleaziest) ways to make money in the waning hours of end-stage capitalism. Far from welcoming bots, ecommerce sites were always going to block them.

It's easy to come up with amazing applications for technology if you're allowed to assume that you can get everyone else in the world to set aside their priorities and their interests in favor of yours. But unless someone has a plan to do that, we shouldn't take them seriously.

title: Why don’t we run the taskbar and Task Manager at high priority, so they can remain responsive?
content:
If a system becomes CPU-starved, all processes begin to suffer. This includes the taskbar and Task Manager, even though they are often the tools you want to use to stop whatever it is that’s making your system suffer. Why can’t we run the taskbar and Task Manager at high priority?

The catch with running anything at high priority is that unless you have been very careful to avoid it, you will eventually run into a shared resource that you will have to wait for, and you are now stuck. Your priority checkout pass gets you to the front of the line, but if the person at the register has a large shopping cart full of groceries, you just have to wait until they are done before you get your chance.

Even if the code that protects the shared resource is careful to avoid priority inversion by transferring the priority of the waiter to the thread that owns the resource, you are still stuck waiting, and that owning thread might be doing something that takes a long time, like, say, accessing a file over the network.

For UI code, this problem is particularly acute because you will eventually have to call into the UI system, and now you’re duking it out with all the other UI threads in the system.

The problem is that it’s hard to fix a runaway system from within that same system. The tools which you can use to try to fix the system may already have been compromised. And it’s definitely hard to fix a runaway system if your tools have to share critical resources with the thing that is out of control. Windows already gives preferential treatment to the program that is in focus, so if you can get focus onto the taskbar or Task Manager, you are doing about as well as you can. But that preferential treatment takes you only so far if those preferred threads find themselves blocked on things that are controlled by non-preferred threads.

The post Why don’t we run the taskbar and Task Manager at high priority, so they can remain responsive? appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: The Unbalanced Group Theorem
content:
The classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) has been called the biggest theorem in mathematics. It is big, not necessarily in terms of its importance, but in the sense that its proof developed over the course of decades and thousands of pages of journal articles.

Two days ago Axiom announced it had formalized the proof of CFSG in 43.1 million lines of Lean. If you click on the link for the accompanying paper, you’ll find that the title of the paper is The Unbalanced Group Theorem, not The Classification of Finite Simple Groups. Why is that?

The unbalanced group theorem (UGT) is a key component of the CFSG. In the course of their effort to formalize CFSG Axiom found counterexamples to an assertion that the 1986 proof of UGT depends on. The UGT, and the CFSG that depends on it, is correct, but the proof was flawed. Axiom formalized the entire CFSG but focused their paper on their new proof of the UGT.

***

What exactly does the UGT say? For that matter, what is a finite simple group?

A short post like this can only go into so much detail, but I’ll see what I can do.

A group represents some kind of symmetry. Groups can be built out of simple groups sorta like the way integers can be built out of primes. See more on the comparison between simple groups and prime numbers here.

The CFSG says that every finite simple group is cyclic, alternating, of Lie type, or sporadic. The UGT is a technical result used in proving that nothing is missing from this list of possibilities.

What does it mean for a group to be “unbalanced”? This depends on a few preliminary definitions.

  • Define O(G) to be the largest normal subgroup of G with an odd number of elements.
  • An element t in G is called an involution if it has order 2: t is not the identity but t² is.
  • The centralizer of an element t of a group G, written CG(t), is the set of elements of G that commute with t.

A group G is unbalanced if O(CG(t)) is a not a subgroup of O(G) for some involution t.

The UGT is a classification theorem for unbalanced groups.

Related posts

  • How big is the monster?
  • Orders of finite simple groups
  • Overlaps in the CFSG
The post The Unbalanced Group Theorem first appeared on John D. Cook.

title: This Week in Source Control: 28 October 2026
content:
Alongside package management, I follow new features and security fixes in source control clients and in the forges that host repositories, since a lot of what I build, like git-pkgs, reads git repositories and calls forge APIs. This Week in Package Management has been published every Saturday since May, and I kept putting git releases and forge news in its Elsewhere section.

Starting this week, I’m publishing that material as a separate roundup on Wednesdays. It covers clients like git, jj, gitoxide, Sapling, Mercurial and Git LFS, and forges like GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo, Gitea, Codeberg, sourcehut, Radicle and Tangled. Package managers resolving git dependencies and CI systems like GitHub Actions are covered in the Saturday post.

This first issue covers the fortnight since 11 October, with links from release feeds for those tools and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News and my boosts on Mastodon. In that fortnight Anthropic, GitHub, Entire and Enroute each published a post about rebuilding source control or git hosting for the volume of pushes and checkouts from coding agents.

Scaling

Redesigning source control at Anthropic (Anthropic Engineering) describes Scion, an in-house version control system that replaced git for the company’s monorepo in five months. Merges went from around 2,500 a day in May to over 30,000 a day in September. The main branch history is almost 100 GB, and CI performs around 25 million checkouts a day. Scion is designed for clients that are always online. The server stores changesets in a write-ahead log on Spanner and runs blame, history and merge queries server-side, and clients fetch only the trees and blobs they request through regional caches. Anthropic reports the new infrastructure uses 200x less CPU and memory than the git mirror fleet it replaced. In notes on the post, Simon Willison compares it to centralised systems like Subversion.

Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke (sunshowers) points out that Scion’s “derived data” for fast blame and history queries matches the design of Mononoke, the server side of Meta’s Sapling. The original post credited Sapling only for “hard-won lessons”. A follow-up compares Scion’s changesets with Mononoke’s Bonsai changesets. Anthropic has since updated its post with more detail on the projects Scion is based on.

The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure (Eleanor White and Victoria Dye, GitHub Blog) covers the move of GitHub’s repositories to Azure. Most repositories have two of their five replicas there, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. Moving the busiest repositories was blocked by a repository-wide lock that every write held across a 25ms cross-region round trip. Spokes is switching to per-reference serialisation, so only writes to the same ref wait for each other, which gave 3-4x write throughput in internal tests. Object storage then joins the write quorum as a “virtual replica”, so read replicas can be stateless.

Entire, a new git forge from a company co-founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, is built for repositories where coding agents and people push to the same branches. Its git server replicates each repository across regions, and the company’s forgemark benchmark reports pushes up to 89x faster than GitHub and 6x faster than Cursor Origin. Review happens through Trails, which run configured checks and agent-run evaluations in Daytona or E2B sandboxes on every push instead of a pull request diff. Agent sessions and prompts are synced into the repository and indexed for later agents to search.

Everyone is doing Git on S3 wrong (Enroute) looks at the write-ahead log designs for git on object storage that followed Cursor’s Continuity. Those designs send every push to a repository through one primary, and every replica keeps a full copy of the repository on disk. Enroute keeps each repository’s refs and a list of immutable object layers in a Raft-replicated log. Packfiles are rewritten on ingestion so a read from object storage needs only a few requests, and Enroute reports more than 7,600 pushes per second into a single repository. Against stock git serving a repacked linux.git, full clones are about 17% slower and shallow clones more than twice as fast.

Releases

GitLab 19.5 makes the GitLab MCP server and GitLab Secrets Manager, built on OpenBao, generally available. Smaller changes include a commit count variable for commit message templates, and commits signed by revoked GPG identities now show as unverified.

Forgejo 17.0 resolves absolute links in rendered documents against the repository root, as other forges do, and deprecates action run webhook events in favour of workflow run events. It also adds a Donate button driven by FUNDING.yml, migration from Bitbucket Data Center, and opt-in invitations for organisation membership. Forgejo 17.0.1, 16.0.7 and 15.0.11 followed on 26 October as security releases. The main fix stops a pull_request_review event running an Actions workflow as trusted from an arbitrary commit, including one from a fork, by ignoring the unvalidated commit_id on the submitted review. 17.0.1 also carries bug fixes for 17.0.0, which the project had advised holding off from after reports of blocked pushes and merges.

GitRoot 0.5.0, a self-hosted forge with no database that is extended through WASM plugins, now references plugins by PURL with a checksum qualifier in place of separate URL, checksum and version fields. New per-forge and per-repository settings cap how many branches anonymous users can push before further anonymous pushes are rejected.

Pushin.eu, an invite-only forge hosted in the EU, shipped several releases this fortnight according to its changelog. 0.3.26 adds tag-based releases with a GitHub-compatible API and GoReleaser publishing, and 0.3.29 serves public repository files from raw.pushin.eu. 0.3.32 adds runner groups for self-hosted runners and removes the per-repository allow_persistent_runners setting.

forges (Daniel Roe) is a TypeScript version of my Go library git-pkgs/forge, with one interface for issues, pull requests, notifications, checks and webhooks across GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Forgejo, Gitea, Gitee, Azure DevOps, Cursor Origin, Tangled, Pushin.eu and Sourcehut. Each provider declares which operations it supports, and the release notes show the capability changes per forge. 0.1.0 came out on 11 October, and 0.3.0 adds branch rules and review threads.

gt 0.1.0 replaces tea, Gitea’s command line tool, with a rewrite under a new name and repository. Every list and view command supports --json and --jq, and gt pr checkout and gt pr diff handle fork and AGit pull requests. It requires Gitea 28 or newer.

gitoxide 0.61.0 moves the plumbing crates to a standard std::error::Error compatible error type and improves tracing across commands, along with security fixes.

Security

Git LFS 3.8.1 fixes four CVEs:

  • unquoted arguments in remote commands sent over SSH
  • Cookie headers forwarded to other hosts after a redirect
  • an arbitrary program run from a malicious repository through line feeds in a submodule URL
  • an arbitrary program run from a malicious repository through a custom transfer adapter set in .lfsconfig

GitLab shipped two critical patch releases for integer overflows in its regular expression compiler that allowed unauthenticated code execution. The first, on 12 October, fixed CVE-2026-97229 in CI configuration patterns, and a 21 October release fixed CVE-2026-110264, which affects every version from 7.0 and was backported as far as 18.11.13. The underlying bugs are in Ruby’s Onigmo, whose fixes were in last week’s package management roundup.

Gitea 28.2.0 discloses 13 CVEs, two of them fixed in earlier releases. One fix limits which stored public keys an SSH certificate principal is matched against. Before the fix, matching against every stored key let a certificate authenticate as a different user.

git-annex 10.20261026 fixes CVE-2026-112818, a cross-repository exfiltration attack found by Joey Hess. A repository the victim clones can autoenable a special remote that points at the victim’s own private git-annex storage, so a later git-annex sync --content reads the private files and sends them to the attacker. After the fix, enableremote requires the special remote’s configuration to be verified, and git-annex refuses to send content to an unverified autoenabled remote.

Gheist (Rami McCarthy and Hila Ramati, Wiz) is a campaign that used stolen GitHub tokens to push a workflow to every reachable repository. The workflow writes repository secrets to its log in base32 so GitHub’s masking leaves them unredacted, and the attacker’s tool fetches the log over the API and deletes the run seconds later. GitHub’s hold on potentially malicious workflows in public repositories, in place since 28 July, blocked the payload there. Private repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server fall outside that hold, and Wiz observed successful runs and follow-on AWS activity from those.

An attacker took over a developer’s GitHub account and replaced OVHcloud CLI releases 0.11.0 to 0.15.0 with builds that read secrets from disk. Release immutability was turned off on the repository, so the attacker could overwrite the existing releases directly and skip CI.

GitHub

Push attribution, in limited preview for Enterprise customers, records the authenticated user who pushed each commit alongside the author and committer fields. A new “Committer must match pusher” ruleset condition accepts a push only when the committer matches one of the pusher’s verified email addresses.

During periods of unusual traffic, unauthenticated HTTPS clones and fetches of public repositories may require authentication, while SSH, authenticated HTTPS and pushes work as before.

GitHub CLI 2.103.0 adds gh auth login --expiring for refreshable tokens that expire within hours. Used as a git credential helper, it requires git 2.46 or newer, which discards a cached credential when it expires.

Repositories can now convert all their branch protection rules to rulesets in one step, with a preview before anything changes. A new repository_creation:write permission lets apps and fine-grained tokens create repositories with only that permission instead of full repository administration.

On the Files changed tab of a pull request, the whitespace visibility setting can be saved so it applies across pull requests, and new and deleted files now span both columns in split view.

Email notifications for push events have been retired because recipients could be added without consenting.

Elsewhere

Haxy, now in preview, is a local-first forge written in Zig that stores issues, pull requests and discussions as events on a haxy/events branch and serves a TUI over SSH alongside its web interface.

Making git hooks visible in fish shell (Chris R) ports Ned Batchelder’s zsh function, which lists a repository’s executable hooks when you cd into it, after Frank Wiles nearly fell for an attack hidden in a shared hooks folder.

jwz has created a GitHub repository whose only content is a README stating that XScreenSaver releases are published only as tarballs on the XScreenSaver website and that other repositories are unofficial.

Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.
description: Releases, advisories, and articles from across version control and forges

title: We Won’t “Just Hang Out”
content:
What will we do after the Singularity? The standard answer is: “we’ll just hang out”. The infinite vacation, as in the Culture novels. I think this won’t work. “Hanging out” implies:

  1. Other people exist.
  2. They want to hang out with you.
  3. You want to hang out with them.

And the post-scarcity, infinite vacation AI utopia undermines all these assumptions.

Other people exist

The social processes by which people come together and build relationships will disappear. Work, obviously, is pointless in a world of cheap superhuman intelligence. University (really all education beyond teaching people to speak) will be pointless because there’s no work to do and because growing your human capital doesn’t change your life outcomes: you get the same UBI whether you’re illiterate or a PhD.

I met a lot of my friends by writing open-source code, and participating in the community of software engineers. AI is dissolving that community by making human contributions superfluous. If Claude Code has existed when I was starting out, nobody would have cared about Austral or my other open-source projects or my technical blog posts.

As a teenager I tried to install Linux, ran into all kinds of problems, and went on the IRC chatrooms to get help. And in the process I made friends. Today, I would just ask Claude. AI disintermediates everyone, so that we no longer need each other. I still have friends, but I’m running off this pre-AI supply of friends I met through communities of practice. Young people don’t have that privilege.

What even is the point of cities in a world without work? If there’s nothing to do, there is no need to bring people together geographically.

They want to hang out with you

The BATNA to hanging out keeps getting better, cheaper, and more convenient. When people’s sensorium becomes an infinite firehose of AI-generated superstimulus, why would they hang out with anyone?

This is less about AI and more about the trajectory of consumer technology, since many people already live like this: they go to work and watch TikTok. After work, they will just watch TikTok.

You want to hang out with them

As Gregory Conti explains:

[Under] ASI this endless leisure will be passed in diminished, tiresome company, since we will lack the experiences of struggle and striving that generate interesting personalities. Our minds will have atrophied. We will have little of note to say to one another.

The people in the AI utopia will have no skills, no education, no accomplishments. We’ll be lucky if they are even literate. They will not be worth talking to, and you won’t want to hang out with them.

Maybe you and I can hang out with our existing friends. But just iterate this a bit. What about the next generation? How are they going to build meaningful relationships where the social processes that built those relationships are all in the past?

If we get radical life extension, there’s the problem of attrition over the long term: people will drift apart, drop out of society to enter the experience machine, die in accidents, or end their lives out of ennui. So your social network might be a non-renewable resource that gets exhausted over time as your pre-Singularity relationships attrite and can’t be replaced for the reasons above.
description: On human connection after the Singularity.
